title: Flight Mechanics
full_title: Flight Mechanics: Performance, Stability and Control
tagline: Aircraft performance, range and endurance, manoeuvres, take-off and landing, static stability and trim, the equations of motion, dynamic modes and flight control
summary: Flight mechanics predicts how an aircraft flies: how fast, how far and how high it can go, whether it is stable, and how it is controlled. The course covers steady-flight performance, range and endurance, turns, take-off and landing, longitudinal and lateral–directional static stability and trim, the rigid-body equations of motion, the dynamic modes of an aircraft and handling qualities, and an introduction to stability augmentation, autopilots and fly-by-wire.
overview: Flight mechanics predicts how an aircraft flies as a whole: how fast, how slowly, how high and how far it can go, whether it returns to its trimmed condition after a disturbance, how it responds to its controls, and what feedback is needed to make it pleasant and safe to fly. It takes the aerodynamic forces of the [[aerodynamics]] course and the thrust and fuel consumption of [[propulsion]] as given, and combines them with Newton's laws for a rigid body. Its results are used every day in aircraft design (sizing the wing, tail and engines), in certification and flight test, in the performance manuals that pilots and airlines use to plan every flight, and in the design of autopilots and fly-by-wire systems.

The course has three parts. The first three lessons treat the aircraft as a particle: the standard atmosphere and airspeeds, the drag polar and the thrust and power required, maximum speed, climb and glide; the Breguet range and endurance equations and the best cruise speeds; and turns, the V–n diagram, take-off and landing. The next two lessons ask whether the trimmed aircraft is statically stable in pitch, yaw and roll — the neutral point and static margin, the elevator angle to trim, the fin and the dihedral effect, and the control needed for crosswinds and engine failures. The last three lessons derive the six-degree-of-freedom equations of motion, linearise them about steady flight into longitudinal and lateral–directional state-space models, compute the five classical modes (short period, phugoid, roll subsidence, spiral and Dutch roll) and judge them against handling-qualities requirements, and finally show how dampers, autopilots and fly-by-wire control laws change them.

Two generic aircraft — a four-seat light aircraft and a narrow-body jet transport — are used throughout, so that each lesson's numbers can be checked against the others. The hard part of the subject is not the mathematics, which is algebra, calculus and the eigenvalues of small matrices, but the bookkeeping: axes and sign conventions, true against equivalent airspeed, weight against mass in fuel consumption, and the many assumptions behind each formula. Each lesson states its assumptions and conventions explicitly; working the examples with a calculator or a few lines of Python, and checking every result for order of magnitude, is the best way to learn the subject.
outcomes: Use the International Standard Atmosphere and convert between true, equivalent and calibrated airspeed in performance calculations.

Calculate the thrust and power required, minimum-drag and minimum-power speeds, maximum speed, rate and angle of climb, ceilings and glide performance of an aircraft from its drag polar and engine data.
Derive and apply the Breguet range and endurance equations for jet and propeller aircraft, choose the best cruise conditions, and construct a payload–range diagram.
Analyse turning and pulling-up flight, construct a V–n diagram, and estimate take-off and landing ground distances.
Determine the neutral point, static margin, trim elevator angle and centre-of-gravity limits of an aircraft, stick-fixed and stick-free.
Evaluate directional stability, dihedral effect, roll damping and control power, and size the rudder and ailerons for crosswind and engine-out conditions.
Derive the rigid-body equations of motion in body axes, linearise them about steady flight, and assemble the longitudinal and lateral–directional state-space models from stability derivatives.
Compute and interpret the short-period, phugoid, roll, spiral and Dutch-roll modes, using both the full models and the classical approximations, and assess them against handling-qualities criteria.
Design simple pitch and yaw dampers and attitude-hold loops, and explain the principles, benefits and risks of relaxed static stability and fly-by-wire control laws.

chapters.title: Steady flight performance
chapters.summary: The standard atmosphere and airspeeds, the equations of steady flight and the drag polar, thrust and power required, minimum drag and minimum power, maximum speed, climb, ceilings and gliding.

chapters.title: Range and endurance
chapters.summary: Specific fuel consumption, the Breguet range and endurance equations for jet and propeller aircraft, cruise programmes, best speeds for range and endurance, wind and the payload–range diagram.

chapters.title: Manoeuvres, take-off and landing
chapters.summary: Load factor, level turns and pull-ups, corner speed, the V–n diagram and gust loads, and take-off and landing ground distances.

chapters.title: Longitudinal static stability and trim
chapters.summary: The pitching moment about the centre of gravity, the neutral point and static margin, trim with the elevator and centre-of-gravity limits, and stick-free stability and stick forces.

chapters.title: Lateral–directional static stability
chapters.summary: Sideslip, directional stability and the fin, the dihedral effect, roll damping and aileron power, and steady asymmetric flight in crosswinds and after an engine failure.

chapters.title: Aircraft equations of motion
chapters.summary: Body axes and Euler angles, the rigid-body equations of motion, linearisation about steady flight, stability derivatives and the longitudinal and lateral state-space models.

chapters.title: Dynamic stability and aircraft modes
chapters.summary: Eigenvalues and mode shapes, the short-period and phugoid modes, roll subsidence, the spiral mode and the Dutch roll, their approximations, and handling-qualities criteria.

chapters.title: Introduction to flight control
chapters.summary: Stability augmentation with pitch and yaw dampers, relaxed static stability, autopilot loops and the principles of fly-by-wire control laws and redundancy.

history.title: Cayley's "On Aerial Navigation"
history.detail: George Cayley's three-part paper in *Nicholson's Journal* (1809–1810) treats the fixed-wing aeroplane as the production of lift against a resisting force, and argues that wings set at an upward angle give stability in roll — the first statement of the dihedral effect.

history.title: The first stability theory
history.detail: G. H. Bryan and W. E. Williams publish "The longitudinal stability of aerial gliders" in the *Proceedings of the Royal Society*, introducing the resistance (stability) derivatives and the quartic stability equation.

history.title: Lanchester's Aerodonetics
history.detail: F. W. Lanchester's *Aerodonetics*, the second volume of his *Aerial Flight*, analyses the long-period oscillation of a glider and names it the phugoid.

history.title: Stability in Aviation
history.detail: Bryan's book sets out the small-disturbance equations of motion in body axes, their separation into longitudinal and lateral sets, and the stability criteria for each — the framework still used today.

history.title: The range equation
history.detail: J. G. Coffin's "A study of airplane ranges and useful loads" (NACA Report No. 69, issued with the NACA's fifth annual report, for 1919) is the earliest published derivation usually cited of what is now called the Breguet range equation.

history.title: Quantitative flying qualities
history.detail: R. R. Gilruth's NACA Report 755, *Requirements for Satisfactory Flying Qualities of Airplanes*, turns pilots' opinions and flight-test measurements into quantitative design criteria.

history.title: The Cooper–Harper scale
history.detail: NASA TN D-5153 by G. E. Cooper and R. P. Harper Jr. standardises the pilot rating scale for handling qualities, from 1 (excellent) to 10 (major deficiencies).

history.title: Digital fly-by-wire
history.detail: NASA's F-8 Digital Fly-By-Wire research aircraft first flies on 25 May, the first fixed-wing aircraft with a digital fly-by-wire system and no mechanical back-up.

history.title: MIL-F-8785C
history.detail: The U.S. military specification *Flying Qualities of Piloted Airplanes* (5 November 1980) sets Level 1–3 requirements on the frequencies, damping and time constants of the aircraft modes; it was later replaced by the MIL-STD-1797 series.

history.title: Airbus A320
history.detail: The A320 first flies on 22 February 1987 and enters service with Air France in April 1988, the first airliner with digital fly-by-wire flight controls and side-stick controllers.

references.title: Aircraft Performance and Design
references.note: McGraw-Hill. Clear, thorough treatment of steady performance, range and endurance, manoeuvres, take-off and landing, with the conceptual-design context; the main reference for the first three lessons.

references.title: Flight Stability and Automatic Control
references.note: 2nd edition (McGraw-Hill). The standard undergraduate text on static stability, the linearised equations, the aircraft modes, handling-qualities criteria and classical autopilot design; this course follows its notation for the dimensional derivatives.

references.title: Dynamics of Flight: Stability and Control
references.authors: Bernard Etkin and Lloyd Duff Reid
references.note: 3rd edition (Wiley). Rigorous derivation of the equations of motion, stability derivatives and modes; the source of the moment equation and neutral-point treatment used here.

references.title: Flight Dynamics Principles
references.note: 3rd edition (Butterworth-Heinemann). A linear-systems approach to flight dynamics with worked examples, mode approximations and an introduction to stability augmentation.

references.title: Aircraft Control and Simulation
references.authors: Brian L. Stevens, Frank L. Lewis and Eric N. Johnson
references.note: 3rd edition (Wiley). Nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom modelling, trimming and simulation, and modern flight-control design; the next step after the last three lessons.

references.title: Mechanics of Flight
references.note: 2nd edition (Wiley). Comprehensive and detailed on performance, static and dynamic stability, with careful derivations and many numerical examples.

references.title: Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach
references.note: 6th edition (AIAA). How the performance and stability results of this course are used to size the wing, tail and engines and to build mission fuel fractions.
